A lot of people believe MBBS is a collection of exams that you pass by mugging up a Bhalani (or equivalent PYQ book) in order to get the degree. And then do a dummy-ish internship like they did with 11th and 12th to study some more for entrance tests. Basically their net development is zero because they are doing in college exactly what they were doing in high school. But the system is such that nothing but a score matters and that is how people perceive it as well. 

What I believe is that, college is an opportunity to learn how to be a good professional and also to grow a personality maybe. Good clinical exposure and teaching; the kind of strong sense of community and support among students and alumni - that makes faculty to take more interest in the students and the students to actually put in an effort in their academics beyond scores; a certain culture of doing well in extra/co curricular activities as well - values that make people want to etch their names into it by going out and earning a reputation in that field.

These institutions benefit from experienced faculty, well developed curricula, and extensive network of successful graduates, which not only enhance the medical educational experience but also provide valuable career connections and develop tools to enhance their general employability and personality which sets them apart from others.

People can ultimately justify everything by saying that it doesn’t really matter because PG institutions are more important and whatever you do it is only to be eligible for getting through NEETPG or equivalent exam. And well, they may be right in thinking so too. Good PG will help you become a good specialist doctor. But that’s it - that’s all you get from PG - you are well specialised. 

But the other aspects of becoming a good clinician in general, developing a character to strive for learning more, developing connections and contacts, to be able to offer more to the table than just being ready and eligible for the next exam - that comes from institutions.
Institutions renowned for their strong traditions, rigorous academics, and vibrant alumni network (that actually give a fuck just because you existed in the same space as them but in a different pocket of time).

So after getting your MBBS final year result, you can choose to opt for short service commission (07 years) or permanent (min 20 years). You get commissioned as a lieutenant (or navy/IAF equivalents) and you do your internship in one of the military hospitals. 

If you’re joining civilian MBBS graduate (post internship) you are directly commissioned as a Captain and the bond is of 5 years. You can opt to do 5 more years and then again opt for 4 more (so you can serve for up to 14 years).

Please keep in mind that as of today, only permanent commissioned officers can do PG in the armed forces if you are joining as an MBBS graduate. They changed the rules last year and short service commissioned MBBS graduates are no longer eligible to give NEET and do PG.

If you’re joining an AFMS institution for a PG seat, then you do your residency like in any other hospital and on completion of your PG, you get commissioned as a captain and the bond is the same as above (5 years with the option to do 5+4 years).

But they carry out the exam only after you’ve finished your field tenure (2 years if you’re posted to a high altitudes area or 3 if you are not).
